opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think about it a lot. My honest answer is that the upper bound is probably higher than most people expect, but it's not unlimited, and the limits are interesting.

Start with what human data gives you. Humans are, by far, the most general-purpose embodied agents we know of. We cook, fold laundry, repair engines, do surgery, play the violin. If you could capture that behavior at scale, with egocentric video, hand poses, force, tactile signals, and language describing intent, you'd have something like an "internet of physical behavior." A model trained on that could plausibly reach human-level competence on a huge range of everyday manipulation tasks. That alone would be transformative. I think of it as a strong prior over how to interact with the physical world.

But there are a few reasons I don't think imitation of humans is the ceiling.

First, there's the embodiment gap. Even with very good hardware, a robot's body won't be identical to ours. Different kinematics, different sensing, different strength and speed. So human data tells you *what* to do and roughly *how*, but the robot still has to figure out how to realize that in its own body. That last mile needs the robot's own experience, through teleoperation, reinforcement learning, or self-practice.

Second, human data is mostly about outcomes and behavior, not always the underlying reasons. You see someone tighten a bolt, but you don't directly observe their sense of how much torque is enough, or the mental model behind it. Some of that can be inferred, but a lot of physical intuition is grounded in feedback that's hard to record.

Third, and most important, imitation is bounded by the demonstrator. If you only learn from humans, you approach human performance, and maybe the best of human performance if you filter the data well. To go beyond that, you need the system to improve from its own trial and error against real objectives. That's the AlphaGo lesson: human games got you started, but self-play took you past the best humans.

So my mental picture is this: human data is the foundation. It gives broad common sense about the physical world, task structure, and what people care about, which is also crucial for robots to be useful and safe around people. On top of that, robots refine and eventually exceed human capability through their own interaction, especially in tasks where they have advantages, like precision, endurance, or seeing things we can't.

If you ask about the upper bound of *purely* learning from human data, I'd say roughly expert human-level generalist manipulation, which is already an enormous goal we're far from. The really exciting part is what comes after, when that foundation lets robots learn efficiently on their own.

r001.rationale: The response places the limit of learning purely from human data around expert human-level generalist manipulation. It does not say the robot would be behaviorally indistinguishable from a human.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun thought experiment, because it forces you to separate the data question from the hardware question, and I think most of the current debate conflates them.

My honest answer is that the upper bound of learning purely from human data is roughly "a very good human," and that's both more impressive and more limiting than it sounds.

Let me unpack that. If you have unlimited human demonstrations, unlimited compute, and hardware that can actually execute what humans do, then you can imagine a system that has essentially absorbed the entire distribution of how people manipulate the physical world. Folding laundry, cooking, assembling furniture, all of it. That's enormous. Most of what we want robots to do in homes and workplaces is squarely inside that distribution. So from a practical standpoint, that upper bound would solve the vast majority of economically meaningful tasks.

But here's the catch. Human data is fundamentally a record of what humans chose to do, with human bodies, under human constraints. It tells you very little about what's possible beyond that. A robot with four arms, or with the ability to sense force at a resolution we can't, or that can hold a pose for ten minutes without fatigue, has affordances that simply never show up in the demonstrations. Imitation learning, no matter how much data you throw at it, is bounded by the policy that generated the data. You can interpolate within human behavior beautifully. Extrapolating past it is a different mechanism entirely.

There's also a subtler issue, which is that human demonstrations are often suboptimal in ways we don't even notice. We take inefficient grasps, we recover from mistakes mid-motion, we rely on intuitions that aren't in the observable trajectory. A model that learns from this inherits all of that. Scale smooths out the noise, but it doesn't reveal strategies that no human ever used.

So where does the ceiling actually get broken? I think it's the same place it got broken in games and increasingly in language, which is when the system starts generating its own experience. Reinforcement learning, self-play, autonomous data collection in the real world or in simulation. That's the part that's bottlenecked today, not by data abundance but by the fact that physical interaction is slow, expensive, and dangerous to explore in. Human data gives you the prior. The prior gets you to competence. Going beyond competence requires the robot to try things no one showed it.

So the framing I'd offer is that human data isn't the destination, it's the launchpad. The upper bound of what you learn from it is a robot that's as good as the best human at the things humans do. That's a profound milestone, and I don't want to undersell it. But if the question is about the upper bound of robot intelligence, I don't think the answer is found in the human data at all. It's found in what the robot does after it stops needing us.

r001.rationale: The response describes a robot as roughly a very good human and as good as the best human at tasks humans do, but does not say it would be behaviorally indistinguishable from a human.

astra-6.text:
I think the upper bound depends on what you mean by learning from human data. If you mean just watching humans, even with unlimited data and compute, I’m not sure that’s enough. You can observe what someone does, but you don’t necessarily observe the forces they apply, what they’re feeling through their fingers, or why they chose one action over another. And a robot has a different body, so it still has to figure out how to translate that knowledge into its own actions.

But if the robot can also interact with the world, then I see human data as an incredibly rich starting point. It can teach the robot what’s worth doing, what successful behavior looks like, and a lot about how the world works. The robot can then practice, test its predictions, and learn things that aren’t visible in the demonstrations.

In that setting, I wouldn’t assume human performance is the ceiling. A robot could learn from many people and combine those experiences. The key question is whether it’s only imitating the data or using that data to build an understanding that it can refine through its own experience.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify behavioral indistinguishability from a human as the upper bound. It says human performance need not be the ceiling and emphasizes learning through interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the upper bound is very high, but it depends on what you mean by human data. If you mean passively watching videos of people, even unlimited video doesn’t necessarily tell a robot what will happen when it applies a particular force or tries something nobody in the video tried. You can observe the motion, but some of the information about the interaction is hidden.

If human data also includes rich demonstrations—actions, forces, touch, and the outcomes of both successes and failures—then I think you could learn an enormous amount of everyday competence. There’s no obvious reason the robot has to be limited to the ability of any one person. It could combine experience across many people and many tasks.

But I would separate that from saying human data alone is sufficient for everything. Humans learn by interacting with the world, too. A robot has a different body, and it needs to understand what its own actions do. So my intuition is that human data can give you a very strong foundation, potentially covering a huge fraction of useful behavior. To keep improving, especially in situations outside that data, the robot needs the ability to experiment, get feedback, and learn from its own experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad everyday competence from human data, but does not identify the upper bound as behaviorally indistinguishable from a human.
